title: Replatforming a site without throwing away search equity
metaTitle: Website migration SEO that protects pages
excerpt: Website migration SEO is an inventory, one-hop redirects, and titles that still describe the page. The work protects familiarity. It does not promise rankings.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky. The buildings stay recognizable from the street, which is the point of keeping known addresses.
caption: Known addresses should still lead somewhere true. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Will a careful migration keep our current rankings?
faqs.answer: Nobody can promise that. Rankings depend on more than your redirects. An inventory, a one-hop redirect to the closest answer, and titles that match the page give the new site a fair chance to inherit the old URLs. Measure what happens after the move instead of treating the launch as a guarantee.

faqs.question: Should old URLs redirect to the homepage?
faqs.answer: Only when the homepage is honestly the closest answer, which is rare. Send each old URL to the new page that covers the same question. A blanket redirect to the homepage strands people who arrived for something specific, and it throws away the meaning of the old address.

faqs.question: When should DNS change?
faqs.answer: Change DNS after staging has passed a sample of redirects, the forms, and a reading of the important pages. Moving the domain first and repairing in public turns the inventory into a fire drill. Keep the old host available long enough to see which paths you missed.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Website migration SEO is the set of moves that keep existing answers findable after the addresses change. The work is an inventory, a redirect for every URL you intend to keep, and titles that still describe the page. It is the practical protection for whatever familiarity the old site had earned. It is not a promise that rankings will hold. Rankings depend on more than a migration, and a guarantee is a guess.

Search equity, in plain words, is the fact that some of your URLs are already the ones people and search engines know. Moving to a new platform without a map throws that familiarity away. The new design can still be the better site. The map is how that site remains reachable from the addresses you already published, printed, and sent in email.

## Make the inventory before you touch the domain

Export every URL that should survive. Include the pages you are proud of and the dull ones: older posts, product pages, policy pages, and any path that receives ads or appears in a signature. Mark each one as keep, merge, or retire.

For a keep, write the new URL. For a merge, write the single new URL that will carry the answer. For a retire, say where a person with a bookmark should land, or why a gone response is the honest one. Three columns are enough: the old URL, the new URL, and the reason.

Do this while the current site is still the live one. Teams that inventory after the new site is called finished discover paths nobody rebuilt. Those paths become gaps. The gaps are where a known address starts returning nothing useful.

Pull the list from the current sitemap, from the host's logs, and from the links you can still find in old campaigns. Logs matter because a page can be quiet in the navigation and busy in practice. A founder almost always forgets at least one URL that a partner has bookmarked. The log is how you catch it before the weekend you switch DNS.

Agree the new URL shape before templates are locked. If every product will live under a new prefix, write that prefix in the sheet and use it.

## Redirects are a map you can test

A redirect sends a request for the old URL to the new one. Use a permanent redirect when the move is real and the new URL should stand in for the old one from here on. Point each old URL at the closest new answer. A redirect of everything to the homepage tells a visitor who wanted a specific page that the page might be somewhere nearby. It tells a search engine very little about that page.

Test the list on a staging host before the domain moves. Request a sample of old paths. Check that each chain is one hop. A redirect that lands on a URL which redirects again adds delay and hides mistakes. Then check the links inside the new pages. Internal links should already use the new paths, so the site is not redirecting itself on every click.

Keep the rules where the project can review them. A file in the repository, read like the rest of the code, is easier to audit than a stack of dashboard entries nobody exports. When Hanabi rebuilds a marketing site on Next.js, those rules ship with the release. They are part of the build, not a souvenir left in the old host's control panel.

Sample more than the homepage. Include a deep page, a merged page, a retired page, and a URL with a trailing variation your old platform may have allowed. Platforms differ on slashes, letter case, and parameters. If the old site answered all of those, the new site needs a decision for each, written in the sheet, or the week after launch fills up with exceptions.

## The new page has to give the same answer

The new URL should answer the question the old URL answered. If a page was useful because it explained shipping times, the new page should still explain shipping times in language a customer can use. A redesign that replaces a clear answer with a slogan has turned the URL into a different, vaguer page. The address can match perfectly and the equity can still drain, because the reason to visit left.

Titles need the same care. [Google Search Central's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says every page should have a title element, that the text should be descriptive and distinct, and that repeated boilerplate makes pages hard to tell apart. Google builds the title link from several sources, including the title element, the visible heading, and other prominent text, and it may choose different wording when the title does not match the page. Give each kept page one obvious heading and a title element that says the same thing. Stuffing the old keyword list into the title to hold a position is the pattern that guidance warns will look spammy.

[Google's notes on people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) are the other half of the check. Helpful pages are created for a person with a job to do, and the main heading should summarize the page. A migration that preserves the URL and drops the explanation has protected a string of characters. The person who arrives still needs the answer they came for. Read the new page as that person, without the design presentation next to it.

Keep one preferred address for each page. The old address points at it. The sitemap lists it. The visible heading, the title element, and the opening paragraph should agree. If the new platform publishes both a trailing-slash version and a bare version, pick one and redirect the other. Two live copies of the same answer split the familiarity you are trying to keep.

## What the work cannot do

The inventory, the redirects, and the titles give the new site a fair chance to inherit the old site's known addresses. They do not freeze a position on a results page. Other sites change. The queries change. The new page may simply be clearer, or worse, than the one it replaced. Measure after the move. Look at which old URLs still receive requests, which redirects fire, and which important pages lost their landing traffic.

Watch the first days for missing pages. A rise in not-found responses means the inventory missed a path. Add the redirect and note it in the sheet so the next migration starts from a better list. A page that loads and says something different from its title needs a copy fix. It does not need a new story about search.

Leave the DNS change until staging has passed the redirect sample, the forms, and a reading of the pages that matter. Moving the domain first, then repairing in public, is how a week disappears. Keep someone available the hour the domain switches. That person is watching logs, not admiring the new type.

A shop has a further constraint: the path a buyer uses to pay has to survive the same weekend. Redirects alone do not prove checkout. Catalog parity, a payment test, and a person watching the first real orders belong in that plan.

## A list you can finish before launch

1. Inventory the old URLs. Mark each as keep, merge, or retire.
2. Write a one-hop redirect to the closest answer.
3. Give each new page a distinct title and the answer the old page gave.
4. Point internal links and the sitemap at the new URLs.
5. Sample the redirects on staging, move DNS, then watch for paths you missed.

Bring the list to the people building the site before the visual design is treated as the whole project. A new template with no map is a new website that happens to use your name. The old addresses are part of the product, because customers and search engines already have them.

If the move includes a store, read [migrating a store without a week of broken checkout](/blog/store-migration-without-broken-checkout) next. The same inventory applies, with payment and catalog truth added to the list.

If you want the map made as part of the rebuild, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio designs and builds the new site and treats the old URLs as part of the job.
